description: Reading Comprehension question bank derived from FDA/SDA General English 17.15 Reading Comprehension. Covers definitions, passage types, reading strategies, main idea, supporting information, inference, vocabulary in context, conclusion, exam strategy, and all three practice passages. Verify and expand with additional passages before formal examination use.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Reading comprehension is best defined as the ability to:

options.A: read a passage quickly without understanding it
options.B: read a passage, understand its meaning and answer questions based on the information presented
options.C: memorise a passage word for word
options.D: translate a passage into another language

questions.explanation: The passage defines reading comprehension as the ability to read a passage, understand its meaning and answer questions based on the information presented.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed among the skills tested by reading comprehension?
questions.explanation: The passage lists understanding, identification of facts, logical reasoning, vocabulary and the ability to draw conclusions. Handwriting improvement is not mentioned.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to the notes, reading comprehension tests vocabulary and the ability to:
questions.explanation: The definition states it tests understanding, identification of facts, logical reasoning, vocabulary and the ability to draw conclusions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How many areas of reading comprehension are listed in the notes?
questions.explanation: The six areas are Passage, Main idea, Supporting information, Inference, Vocabulary in context, and Conclusion.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six areas of reading comprehension listed?
questions.explanation: Punctuation is not among the six areas: Passage, Main idea, Supporting information, Inference, Vocabulary in context, Conclusion.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A passage is defined in the notes as:

options.A: a single sentence stating a fact
options.B: a written paragraph or group of paragraphs dealing with a particular subject

questions.explanation: The passage is defined as a written paragraph or group of paragraphs dealing with a particular subject.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Questions on a passage may test:

options.A: only the passage as a whole
options.C: the passage as a whole or a particular sentence, fact, word or implication

questions.explanation: Questions may test the passage as a whole or a particular sentence, fact, word or implication.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A passage that describes a person, place, object or event is called:
questions.explanation: Descriptive passages describe a person, place, object or event.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.1 Common types of passages

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A passage that tells a story or describes a sequence of events is:
questions.explanation: Narrative passages tell a story or describe a sequence of events.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.1 Common types of passages

questions.subject: English
questions.question: An expository passage primarily:

options.C: explains a subject or provides information
options.D: presents a position supported by reasons

questions.explanation: Expository passages explain a subject or provide information.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.1 Common types of passages

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which passage type presents a position supported by reasons and evidence?
questions.explanation: Argumentative passages present a position supported by reasons and evidence.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.1 Common types of passages

questions.subject: English
questions.question: An analytical passage:

options.B: examines an issue and explains causes, effects or relationships

questions.explanation: Analytical passages examine an issue and explain causes, effects or relationships.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.1 Common types of passages

questions.subject: English
questions.question: An informative passage provides:
questions.explanation: Informative passages provide facts, details and general knowledge.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.1 Common types of passages

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a passage type with its characteristic?

options.B: Argumentative — presents a position supported by reasons and evidence

questions.explanation: Argumentative passages present a position supported by reasons and evidence.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.1 Common types of passages

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to the notes, the first step in reading a passage with a title is to:

options.B: read the title to identify the general topic

questions.explanation: The notes advise reading the title, if provided, to identify the general topic.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.2 How to read a passage

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Why should the entire passage be read once before answering?
questions.explanation: Reading the entire passage once helps understand its overall meaning.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.2 How to read a passage

questions.subject: English
questions.question: While reading a passage, a reader should notice all of the following EXCEPT:

options.D: the font style of the passage

questions.explanation: The notes list names, dates, facts, reasons, examples, contrasts and the author's purpose — not font style.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.2 How to read a passage

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When a question asks what the passage states, the reader should:
questions.explanation: The notes state: answer from the passage when the question asks what the passage states; do not substitute outside knowledge.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.2 How to read a passage

questions.subject: English
questions.question: After reading each question carefully, what should the reader do before choosing an answer?

options.A: Return to the relevant part of the passage to verify the answer

questions.explanation: The notes advise returning to the relevant part of the passage to verify the answer.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 1.2 How to read a passage

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Skimming is defined as:

options.A: reading quickly to understand the general meaning and main idea
options.B: searching quickly for a specific fact

questions.explanation: Skimming means reading quickly to understand the general meaning and main idea.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Scanning is best described as:

options.B: searching quickly for specific information such as a name, date, number, place or fact

questions.explanation: Scanning means searching quickly for specific information such as a name, date, number, place or particular fact.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: For a main-idea question, the recommended technique is to:

options.B: skim and understand the overall message

questions.explanation: The notes advise: for a main-idea question, skim and understand the overall message.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: For a question about a date or name, the best technique is to:
questions.explanation: The notes state: for a question about a date or name, scan for the relevant detail.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: The main idea of a passage answers which question?

options.A: What is the meaning of this word?
options.B: What is this passage mainly about?

questions.explanation: The main idea is the central message and answers: What is this passage mainly about?

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of the main idea?

options.B: It covers the passage as a whole rather than one isolated sentence
options.C: It introduces new information not discussed by the author
options.D: It is narrower than a supporting fact

questions.explanation: The main idea covers the passage as a whole rather than one isolated sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which statement about the main idea is FALSE according to the notes?

options.A: It may be directly stated or implied
options.B: It should not introduce information the author has not discussed
options.C: It is narrower than an individual example
options.D: It represents the central topic of the passage

questions.explanation: The main idea is broader than an individual example or supporting fact, not narrower.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: The main idea of a passage may be:
questions.explanation: The notes state the main idea may be directly stated or implied.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A main idea gives the central message, while a supporting detail:

options.A: explains or supports the central message
options.D: is always longer than the main idea

questions.explanation: Supporting details explain or support the central message.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 2.2 Main idea versus supporting detail

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A supporting detail typically deals with:
questions.explanation: A supporting detail deals with a particular aspect, whereas the main idea covers the passage broadly.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 2.2 Main idea versus supporting detail

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Read: 'Trees are essential for maintaining ecological balance. They absorb carbon dioxide, release oxygen, provide shelter to species and help prevent soil erosion.' What is the main idea?

options.C: Trees are essential for environmental balance

questions.explanation: The main idea is that trees are essential for environmental balance; the individual functions are supporting details.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In the trees example, 'They absorb carbon dioxide' is an example of:
questions.explanation: Individual functions such as absorbing carbon dioxide are supporting details.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is a recommended step for identifying the main idea?
questions.explanation: The method includes identifying the subject discussed repeatedly.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When choosing the main idea, the reader should separate the central message from:
questions.explanation: The method includes separating the central message from examples and minor facts.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is a common question form for the main idea?

options.A: What does this word mean here?
options.B: What is the passage mainly about?

questions.explanation: 'What is the passage mainly about?' is a common main-idea question form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common main-idea question form listed?

options.C: What is the author's primary purpose?
options.D: What is the synonym of the underlined word?

questions.explanation: The synonym question belongs to vocabulary in context, not main idea.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: An option may be factually correct but still wrong for a main-idea question because it:

options.B: describes only one supporting detail, not the passage's main idea

questions.explanation: The exam trap: an option may be factually correct but wrong because it describes only one supporting detail, not the main idea.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Supporting information consists of:

options.A: facts, examples, explanations, reasons, statistics and descriptions

questions.explanation: Supporting information consists of facts, examples, explanations, reasons, statistics and descriptions that develop or strengthen the main idea.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Facts are described as information that:
questions.explanation: Facts provide information that can be checked; e.g., India became independent in 1947.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 3.1 Types of supporting information

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which type of supporting information provides numerical evidence?
questions.explanation: Statistics provide numerical evidence.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 3.1 Types of supporting information

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Comparisons as supporting information are used to:
questions.explanation: Comparisons show similarities or differences.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 3.1 Types of supporting information

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Reasons as supporting information are used to:
questions.explanation: Reasons explain why something happens.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 3.1 Types of supporting information

questions.subject: English
questions.question: 'Solar and wind energy are renewable sources' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The notes use this as an example that explains an idea.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 3.1 Types of supporting information

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Explicit information is information that is:
questions.explanation: Explicit information is directly stated in the passage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Read: 'Drinking sufficient water helps maintain normal body functions.' What helps maintain normal body functions?
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states drinking sufficient water helps maintain normal body functions.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: The first step in locating supporting details is to:

options.A: identify the keyword in the question

questions.explanation: The method begins with identifying the keyword in the question.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: After identifying the keyword, the reader should:

options.A: search for that keyword or a synonym in the passage

questions.explanation: The reader should search for that keyword or a synonym in the passage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When checking options for a supporting-detail question, the reader should reject options that:

options.A: exaggerate, reverse or alter the original statement

questions.explanation: The notes advise rejecting options that exaggerate, reverse or alter the original statement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A fact that is generally true but absent from the passage is:

options.B: not necessarily the correct answer when the question asks what the passage states

questions.explanation: A fact that is generally true but absent from the passage is not necessarily the correct answer when the question asks what the passage states.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: An inference is best defined as:

options.B: a logical conclusion drawn from information in the passage, even when not directly stated
options.C: a direct quotation from the passage

questions.explanation: An inference is a logical conclusion drawn from information in the passage, even when that conclusion is not directly stated.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Drawing an inference requires:

options.A: combining clues with reasonable logical understanding

questions.explanation: Inference requires combining clues with reasonable logical understanding.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A direct statement is information that is:
questions.explanation: Direct statement information is explicitly mentioned.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 4.1 Direct statement versus inference

questions.subject: English
questions.question: An inference is information that is:

options.C: always located directly in the passage

questions.explanation: Inference information is logically suggested.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 4.1 Direct statement versus inference

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A direct statement answers what the author says, while an inference answers:
questions.explanation: An inference answers what the information implies.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 4.1 Direct statement versus inference

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Read: 'The farmers had been waiting for rain for several weeks and continued preparing their fields.' What is the direct information?

options.B: They had waited several weeks for rain

questions.explanation: The direct information is that they had waited several weeks for rain.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: From 'The farmers had been waiting for rain for several weeks and continued preparing their fields,' what is a reasonable inference?

options.B: Rainfall was important for their agricultural activities

questions.explanation: A reasonable inference is that rainfall was important for their agricultural activities.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A logical inference is a conclusion based on:
questions.explanation: A logical inference is a conclusion based on stated facts.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: If everyone who completes a course receives a certificate, and Ravi completes it, what can be logically inferred?

options.B: Ravi will not receive a certificate

questions.explanation: This is the logical inference example given in the notes.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A cause-and-effect inference identifies:

options.A: a likely relationship between an event and its result
options.B: the dictionary meaning of a word

questions.explanation: Cause-and-effect inference identifies a likely relationship between an event and its result.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Author's attitude in a passage may be identified as all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Author's attitude may be supportive, critical, concerned, neutral, optimistic or pessimistic — not grammatical.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When making a prediction, the reader should:

options.B: determine what may happen based on the information supplied

questions.explanation: Prediction means determining what may happen based on the information supplied; do not turn a possibility into certainty.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a rule for inference questions?

options.A: Use information supported by the passage

questions.explanation: The rules include using information supported by the passage.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 4.3 Rules and common traps

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which words should a reader be cautious about in inference options?
questions.explanation: The notes advise being cautious with extreme words such as all, none, always, never and completely.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 4.3 Rules and common traps

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to the rules, a reader should avoid assumptions based on:
questions.explanation: The rules state: avoid assumptions based on personal experience.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 4.3 Rules and common traps

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a common inference trap?

options.A: Selecting outside knowledge that the passage neither states nor implies

questions.explanation: A common trap is selecting outside knowledge that the passage neither states nor implies.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 4.3 Rules and common traps

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A reader must distinguish an author's opinion from:
questions.explanation: The rules include distinguishing an author's opinion from an established fact.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 4.3 Rules and common traps

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Vocabulary in context means identifying the meaning of a word according to:

options.A: how it is used in a particular passage

questions.explanation: Vocabulary in context means identifying the meaning of a word or expression according to how it is used in a particular passage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A word can have several meanings; what determines the appropriate sense?
questions.explanation: Surrounding information determines the appropriate sense of a word.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a type of context clue?
questions.explanation: The listed clues are definition, synonym, antonym, example, explanation and cause/effect. Alliteration is not listed.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: 'An organism that feeds on dead organic matter is called a decomposer.' This is an example of which clue?
questions.explanation: The passage directly explains the word, making it a definition clue.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'An organism that feeds on dead organic matter is called a decomposer,' what does decomposer mean?

options.A: An organism that breaks down dead organic matter

questions.explanation: Decomposer = an organism that breaks down dead organic matter.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: 'The old building was abandoned; nobody lived in it anymore.' This is an example of which clue?
questions.explanation: A similar word or phrase ('nobody lived in it anymore') gives a meaning clue — a synonym clue.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'The old building was abandoned; nobody lived in it anymore,' what does abandoned mean?
questions.explanation: Abandoned = deserted or left unused.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: 'Unlike his generous brother, Ravi was miserly and disliked spending money.' This is an example of which clue?
questions.explanation: The opposite word 'generous' helps establish the meaning — an antonym clue.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'Unlike his generous brother, Ravi was miserly and disliked spending money,' what does miserly mean?
questions.explanation: Miserly = unwilling to spend money; stingy.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: 'The road was slippery because it was covered with ice.' This is an example of which clue?
questions.explanation: The cause or result helps reveal the meaning — a cause/effect clue.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'The road was slippery because it was covered with ice,' what does slippery mean?

options.A: Difficult to walk or drive on without sliding

questions.explanation: Slippery = difficult to walk or drive on without sliding.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Denotation refers to:

options.A: the literal or dictionary meaning of a word
options.B: the emotional association of a word

questions.explanation: Denotation is the literal or dictionary meaning of a word.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Connotation refers to:

options.A: the additional emotional or associated meaning of a word

questions.explanation: Connotation is the additional emotional or associated meaning of a word.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Both 'slim' and 'skinny' describe a thin person, but 'slim' often has:
questions.explanation: Slim often has a positive or neutral connotation, while skinny may suggest excessive thinness.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which word may suggest excessive thinness?
questions.explanation: Skinny may suggest excessive thinness, unlike slim.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is a common vocabulary-in-context question form?

options.A: What is the passage mainly about?
options.B: Choose the synonym or antonym of the underlined word

questions.explanation: 'Choose the synonym or antonym of the underlined word' is a common vocabulary question form.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the exam rule for vocabulary questions?

options.A: Automatically choose the most common dictionary meaning
options.B: Choose the meaning that fits the particular sentence

questions.explanation: The exam rule is: do not automatically choose the most common dictionary meaning; choose the meaning that fits the particular sentence.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A conclusion is best defined as:

options.A: the final understanding or logical outcome derived from the information presented

questions.explanation: A conclusion is the final understanding or logical outcome derived from the information presented in the passage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A stated conclusion is one where:

options.A: the author directly expresses the final message

questions.explanation: A stated conclusion is directly expressed by the author.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: 'Plastic waste harms marine life. Therefore, reducing plastic pollution is essential.' This is an example of:
questions.explanation: The author directly expresses the final message, making it a stated conclusion.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: An implied conclusion is one where:

options.A: the author does not directly state it, but the facts support it
options.C: the reader uses outside knowledge only

questions.explanation: An implied conclusion is not directly stated but is supported by the facts.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Villages using rainwater harvesting report improved groundwater availability. What is a reasonable conclusion?

options.A: Rainwater harvesting can help address water shortages

questions.explanation: A reasonable conclusion is that rainwater harvesting can help address water shortages — the implied conclusion example from the notes.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A recommendation-based conclusion occurs when the passage:

options.A: describes a problem and suggests action

questions.explanation: A recommendation-based conclusion describes a problem and suggests action.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: 'Improving access to education requires collective effort' is an example of:
questions.explanation: The passage describes a problem and suggests action — a recommendation-based conclusion.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: How does an inference differ from a conclusion?

options.A: An inference is a logical understanding drawn from clues, while a conclusion is a final judgement or overall outcome
options.C: An inference is always stated, a conclusion never is
options.D: A conclusion occurs only at the start of reasoning

questions.explanation: An inference is a logical understanding drawn from clues; a conclusion is a final judgement or overall outcome.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A conclusion usually represents:
questions.explanation: A conclusion usually represents the final understanding.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is a recommended step for identifying the correct conclusion?
questions.explanation: The steps include identifying the main idea, reviewing supporting information, determining relationships, identifying the author's final message and rejecting unsupported or extreme conclusions.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 6.3 How to identify the correct conclusion

questions.subject: English
questions.question: When identifying a conclusion, a reader should reject conclusions that:

options.A: introduce unsupported information or extreme claims

questions.explanation: The notes advise rejecting conclusions that introduce unsupported information or extreme claims.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 6.3 How to identify the correct conclusion

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A 'Passage' type question tests:
questions.explanation: Passage questions test overall understanding, e.g., 'What is the text about?'
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 7. Quick Comparison of Question Types

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which question type tests explicit facts and details?
questions.explanation: Supporting information questions test explicit facts and details.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 7. Quick Comparison of Question Types

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which question type tests meaning in a sentence?
questions.explanation: Vocabulary in context tests meaning in a sentence.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 7. Quick Comparison of Question Types

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which question type tests the overall outcome?
questions.explanation: Conclusion questions test the overall outcome.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 7. Quick Comparison of Question Types

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which question type asks 'What is the passage mainly about?'
questions.explanation: 'What is the passage mainly about?' is a main-idea question.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 7. Quick Comparison of Question Types

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 1, what is the main idea of the passage?

options.A: The importance of forests in maintaining ecological balance and the need to protect them
options.C: The role of urbanisation in agriculture
options.D: The chemical composition of carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: The main idea is the importance of forests in maintaining ecological balance and the need to protect them; it summarises the entire passage, not just one forest function.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q1

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 1, which gas do forests absorb?
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that forests absorb carbon dioxide.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q2

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 1, how do forests help protect the soil?

options.A: Their presence helps prevent soil erosion
options.D: They remove minerals from the soil

questions.explanation: This is directly stated: forests protect soil from erosion.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q3

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In Passage 1, what does the word 'deforestation' mean?

options.B: The cutting down or large-scale removal of forests

questions.explanation: Deforestation means the cutting down or large-scale removal of forests in the environmental context.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q4

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which activities are identified as causes of deforestation in Passage 1?

options.A: Agricultural expansion, urbanisation and illegal logging

questions.explanation: All three causes — agricultural expansion, urbanisation and illegal logging — are listed in the passage.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q5

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What can be inferred about forest protection from Passage 1?

options.A: Forest protection requires cooperation between governments and local communities
options.B: Forest protection is the sole responsibility of governments

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly recommends joint action by governments and local communities; this is also the logical implication.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q6

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the author's main recommendation in Passage 1?

options.A: Protect existing forests, encourage afforestation and practise sustainable forest management

questions.explanation: These actions are stated in the final part of the passage.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q7

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which is the most appropriate title for Passage 1?
questions.explanation: 'Forests and Ecological Balance' covers the passage's central subject.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q8

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 1, forests help regulate:
questions.explanation: Forests absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, helping regulate the composition of the atmosphere.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 1, forests provide shelter to:
questions.explanation: The passage states forests provide shelter to wildlife.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which word in Passage 1 is closest in meaning to 'afforestation'?
questions.explanation: Afforestation means planting or establishing forests, encouraged as a protective measure in the passage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 1, sustainable forest management is essential for:

options.A: preserving biodiversity and maintaining environmental stability

questions.explanation: The passage states sustainable forest management is essential for preserving biodiversity and maintaining environmental stability.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which statement is NOT supported by Passage 1?
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly identifies causes of deforestation (agricultural expansion, urbanisation, illegal logging), so saying it has no causes is unsupported.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In Passage 1, 'ecological balance' most nearly means:

options.A: a stable relationship among living things and their environment
options.B: the financial balance of a country
options.C: the number of trees in a city

questions.explanation: Ecological balance refers to a stable relationship among living things and their environment, as used in the passage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: What is the central idea of Passage 2?

options.A: The role of education in individual and social development, and the need to improve equal access and learning quality
options.B: The history of schools in India

questions.explanation: The central idea includes benefits, barriers and improvements — the role of education in development and the need to improve equal access and learning quality.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q9

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of education mentioned in Passage 2?
questions.explanation: The passage lists knowledge, critical thinking, informed decisions, employment opportunities and economic independence as benefits.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q10

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of education in Passage 2?
questions.explanation: The passage mentions employment opportunities but not guaranteed government employment.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 2, what are the reasons for unequal access to education?

options.A: Poverty, inadequate infrastructure and social barriers
options.B: Excessive teachers and too many schools

questions.explanation: The passage lists poverty, inadequate infrastructure and social barriers as reasons for unequal access.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q11

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In Passage 2, what does 'infrastructure' mean?

options.A: Basic facilities and systems needed for education, such as school buildings, classrooms and learning resources

questions.explanation: Infrastructure means basic facilities and systems needed for education — school buildings, classrooms and learning resources.
questions.source: 17.15 Reading Comprehension — 8. Practice Passages / Answer Key Q12

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to the quick revision, the correct answer for inference and conclusion questions must be:
questions.explanation: For inference and conclusion questions, choose only what follows logically from the text.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Passage 1 suggests that protecting forests requires cooperation between:
questions.explanation: The passage states governments and local communities must work together to protect existing forests.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 1, what do forests release after absorbing carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: The passage states forests absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 2, education improves people's ability to make informed decisions and develops:
questions.explanation: The passage states education develops critical thinking and improves decision-making.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 2, which of the following is NOT listed as a reason for unequal access to education?
questions.explanation: The passage lists poverty, inadequate infrastructure and social barriers — not excessive resources.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 3, which of the following is NOT a challenge of technology?
questions.explanation: Faster communication is a benefit, not a challenge. The challenges are privacy risks, cybercrime and misleading information.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: According to Passage 3, users should protect their personal information, verify online content and:
questions.explanation: The passage advises users to protect personal information, verify online content and use digital platforms responsibly.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: A passage states: 'Public transport reduces traffic congestion, lowers pollution and saves fuel.' What is the main idea?

options.A: Public transport has several environmental and practical benefits

questions.explanation: The main idea covers all the benefits; each individual benefit is a supporting detail.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: In 'Public transport reduces traffic congestion, lowers pollution and saves fuel,' 'lowers pollution' is:
questions.explanation: Lowering pollution is one supporting detail of the main idea about public transport benefits.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: From 'Public transport reduces traffic congestion, lowers pollution and saves fuel,' what can be inferred?

options.A: Public transport is beneficial for cities

questions.explanation: The stated benefits logically imply public transport is beneficial for cities.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: From 'Public transport reduces traffic congestion, lowers pollution and saves fuel,' what is a reasonable conclusion?
questions.explanation: The benefits support the recommendation-based conclusion that cities should promote public transport.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Read: 'The committee reached a consensus, with all members agreeing on the plan.' What does 'consensus' mean?
questions.explanation: The context 'all members agreeing' indicates consensus means general agreement.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Read: 'The report was comprehensive, covering every aspect of the issue.' What does 'comprehensive' mean?
questions.explanation: The context 'covering every aspect' indicates comprehensive means complete and covering everything.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Read: 'The new evidence undermined the earlier theory, weakening its support.' What does 'undermined' mean?
questions.explanation: The context 'weakening its support' indicates undermined means weakened.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Read: 'Households that segregated waste reported cleaner neighbourhoods, while those that did not reported more litter.' What is a reasonable conclusion?

options.A: Waste segregation can help keep neighbourhoods clean

questions.explanation: The contrasting facts support the implied conclusion that waste segregation can help keep neighbourhoods clean.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Read: 'The village well dried up, and villagers had to walk several kilometres for water.' What can be inferred?

options.A: The villagers faced a water shortage
options.B: The villagers had plenty of water

questions.explanation: A dried-up well and long walks for water logically suggest a water shortage.

questions.subject: English
questions.question: Which of the following statements about reading comprehension is TRUE according to the notes?

options.A: The correct answer must be supported by the passage
options.D: The longest option is usually correct

questions.explanation: The final exam principle: the correct answer must be supported by the passage.
